entry: Termination of a [[Marriage|marriage]]. Divorce usually entails canceling or reorganizing the legal duties and responsibilities of marriage under the law of the relevant country or state. In most countries it requires the sanction of a court or other authority and may settle property distribution, child custody, alimony, child visitation, child support and division of debt. Because [[Monogamy|monogamy]] is required by law in most countries, divorce allows each former partner to marry another person. It differs from annulment, which declares a marriage null and void, and from legal or de facto separation. Jurisdictions take a fault-based or no-fault approach, and many offer both. In some countries, including Sweden, Finland, Australia and New Zealand, divorce is purely no-fault. The [[Philippines]] and [[Vatican City]] are the only countries that do not allow divorce, although in the Philippines divorce for non-Muslim Filipinos is legal only if one spouse is an undocumented immigrant and certain conditions are met.

Hindu festival of lights, with variations celebrated in [[Jainism]] and [[Sikhism]]. It is associated with the victory of [[Dharma]] over *Adharma*, light over darkness, good over evil and knowledge over ignorance. Diwali falls in the Hindu lunisolar months of *Ashvin* and *Kartika*, between mid-October and mid-November, and its celebrations generally last five or six days. Families illuminate homes, temples and workplaces with *diyas* (oil lamps), candles and lanterns. Hindus take a ritual oil bath at dawn each day of the festival, and the holiday is marked with fireworks, *rangoli* floor designs and shared *mithai*. The main day, [[Lakshmi]] Puja, is an official holiday in Fiji, Guyana, India, Malaysia, Mauritius, Myanmar, Nepal, Pakistan, Singapore, Sri Lanka, Suriname, and Trinidad and Tobago. Jains mark the final liberation of [[Mahavira]], and Sikhs celebrate *Bandi Chhor Divas*, commemorating the release of Guru Hargobind from a Mughal prison.

Belgian-born [[Jazz|jazz]] guitarist and composer. Born Jean Reinhardt into a French family of Romani descent, he was known by the nickname Django. He taught himself the violin, banjo-guitar and guitar as a youth and was able to earn a living busking in cafés by age 15. In 1928 a fire in his caravan severely burned his left hand, and he adapted by fretting mainly with his index and middle fingers. In 1934 he formed the Paris-based Quintette du Hot Club de France with violinist Stéphane Grappelli, one of the first groups to feature the guitar as a lead instrument. He pioneered gypsy jazz, fusing Romani folk traditions with American swing, and his compositions "Minor Swing" and "Nuages" became standards in the genre. Reinhardt briefly toured the United States with [[Duke Ellington]]'s orchestra in 1946.

Rope-tuned, skin-covered goblet drum played with bare hands and widely used in [[West Africa]]. Its name comes from the Bambara saying *Anke djé, anke bé*, meaning "everyone gather together in peace," which reflects its communal purpose. The drum has a hardwood shell and a goatskin head, and it can produce a wide variety of sounds, loud enough to be heard clearly as a solo instrument over a large percussion ensemble. Its origin is associated with the Mandinka blacksmith caste known as the Numu, and the traditional distribution of the drum is associated with the [[Mali Empire]], which dates to 1230 CE. Traditionally it is played only by men, and women playing it are rare in West Africa. A player is called a *djembefola*, a term that does not imply a particular level of skill.

Country in the [[Horn of Africa]], on the [[Red Sea]] and the [[Gulf of Aden]]. It is bordered by [[Somalia]], [[Ethiopia]] and [[Eritrea]], and has an area of 23,200 km2. In antiquity the territory was part of the [[Land of Punt]]. It gained independence from France in 1977, after a referendum, and joined the [[United Nations]] in its first year. Its population was 1,066,809 at the census of May 20, 2024, the smallest in mainland Africa. French and Arabic are official languages, and about 94% of Djiboutians adhere to Islam. The country controls access between the Red Sea and the Indian Ocean and serves as the principal maritime port for Ethiopia's imports and exports. It hosts several foreign military bases and the headquarters of the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD).

Soviet-era Russian composer and pianist. Internationally known after the premiere of his First [[Symphony]] in 1926, he was regarded as a major composer. His 1934 opera *Lady Macbeth of Mtsensk* was initially successful but was later condemned by the Soviet government, and his work was denounced under the Zhdanov Doctrine in 1948. His censure was rescinded in 1956. He chaired the RSFSR Union of Composers from 1960 to 1968 and was a member of the Supreme Soviet of the RSFSR and, from 1962, of the [[Soviet Union]]. His music combines sharp contrasts, grotesque elements and ambivalent tonality, and was influenced by neoclassicism and by [[Gustav Mahler]]. His output includes 15 symphonies, 15 string quartets and six concerti. Scholars continue to debate the relationship between his music and his attitudes toward the Soviet government.

Russian lawyer and politician, president of Russia (2008–2012). Some analysts saw him as more liberal than his predecessor [[Vladimir Putin]], and he presided over Russia's recovery from the [[Great Recession]] and the [[Russo-Georgian War]]. During his term the [[United States]] and Russia signed the New START nuclear arms reduction treaty. He then served as prime minister from 2012 to 2020 and has been deputy chairman of the Security Council since 2020. Since the prelude to the Russian invasion of [[Ukraine]], he has taken increasingly hawkish positions toward the West.

Major river of Eastern Europe, also known as the Dnipro. Rising in the Valdai Hills near Smolensk, [[Russia]], it flows about 2,200 km (1,400 mi) through [[Belarus]] and [[Ukraine]] to the [[Black Sea]]. Its drainage basin covers 504,000 square kilometers (195,000 sq mi), and it is the longest river of Ukraine and Belarus and the fourth-longest in Europe, after the Volga, Danube and Ural rivers. In antiquity it was part of the Amber Road trade routes. During the Soviet period it became known for major hydroelectric dams and large reservoirs. During the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine, sections of the river formed defensive lines. The [[Chernobyl disaster]] of 1986 occurred on the Pripyat River, a tributary of the Dnieper, just upstream from its confluence with the Dnieper.

City in eastern [[Ukraine]], administrative center of Dnipropetrovsk Oblast. It is Ukraine's fourth-largest city, with about one million inhabitants, located 391 km (243 mi) southeast of [[Kyiv]] on the Dnipro River, from which it takes its name. Cossack communities settled the site from at least 1524. Yekaterinoslav, meaning "glory of Catherine," was established as the administrative center of Novorossiya under a decree of [[Catherine the Great]]. From the late 19th century the town attracted foreign capital and a multi-ethnic workforce exploiting [[Donbas|Donbas]] coal and Kryvbas iron ore. Renamed Dnipropetrovsk in 1926 after Grigory Petrovsky, it became a center of heavy industry in the [[Soviet Union]], including nuclear, arms and space industries. More than a third of the population was Jewish until the German occupation in [[World War II]]. It was renamed Dnipro in 2016 during decommunization, and after Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 it became a logistical hub for humanitarian aid.

headword: Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?
sort_key: do androids dream of electric sheep
entry: 1968 dystopian science fiction novel by [[Philip K. Dick]]. Set in a post-apocalyptic [[San Francisco]] after a global war, it follows bounty hunter Rick Deckard, who must "retire" six escaped Nexus-6 [[Android (robot)|androids]]. The novel also features Mercerism, a quasi-religion practiced through empathy boxes. It served as the basis for the 1982 film *Blade Runner*, directed by [[Ridley Scott]], and its cultural significance grew with the film.

1989 American comedy-drama film written and directed by [[Spike Lee]]. Set over one hot summer day in Bedford-Stuyvesant, [[Brooklyn]], it portrays racial tension between African-American residents and Italian-American pizzeria owners. The film grossed $37.3 million worldwide against a budget of $6.2 million. Its ambiguous and controversial conclusion sparked debate about protest, responsibility and moral judgment. It earned [[Academy Awards|Academy Award]] nominations for Best Original Screenplay and Best Supporting Actor, and in 1999 the [[Library of Congress]] selected it for the National Film Registry.

American dentist, gambler and gunfighter in the Old West. A close friend of lawman [[Wyatt Earp]], he saved Earp's life in a Texas saloon and took part in the [[Gunfight at the O.K. Corral]] at Tombstone, Arizona. Popular accounts credit him with more than a dozen killings, but modern researchers conclude that he killed between one and three men. Soon after setting up practice in Georgia, he was diagnosed with [[Tuberculosis]], and he moved west in search of a drier climate, becoming a gambler. He spent his last years in Colorado, where he died.

Human-made structure for handling [[Ship|ships]], usually on or near a shore. In American English, a dock is technically synonymous with a [[Pier|pier]] or wharf, although pier generally refers to structures originally intended for industry. In British English, a dock is an enclosed area of water used for loading, unloading, building or repairing ships. A wet dock holds water with gates or a lock so that ships stay afloat at low tide. The first enclosed wet dock with lock gates was the Howland Great Dock on the [[River Thames]], built in 1703. The first commercial enclosed wet dock, the Old Dock at [[Liverpool]], opened in 1715 and held up to 100 ships. A drydock can be emptied of water for maintenance of a ship's underwater parts. The earliest known docks, from the reign of Pharaoh Khufu, date to about 2500 BC in Egypt, and a dock at Lothal in [[India]] dates from 2400 BC.

British science fiction television series, first broadcast by the [[BBC]] in 1963. It follows the Doctor, a rogue Time Lord from the planet Gallifrey who travels through space and time in the TARDIS, a spaceship whose exterior resembles a British police box. The series was created by Sydney Newman, C. E. Webber and Donald Wilson. Its original run lasted from 1963 to 1989, and it was relaunched in 2005 with production based in [[Cardiff]]. Fourteen actors have played the Doctor, and the changes of actor are explained through regeneration, in which a Time Lord's body renews itself when fatally injured or weakened by age. The Doctor usually travels with companions. The series has been listed in [[Guinness World Records]] as the longest-running science-fiction television series in the world.

Terminal [[Academic degree|academic degree]], usually the highest level of achievement in a discipline. It is awarded after graduate study and original [[Research|research]] that expands the boundaries of knowledge, normally presented in a dissertation and sometimes defended before a panel of experts. The Latin name *philosophiae doctor* uses *philosophy* in the broad Greek sense of "love of wisdom"; in much of Europe, fields other than theology, law and medicine were traditionally known as philosophy. The research doctorate emerged in 19th-century [[Germany]], and [[Yale University]] granted the first U.S. PhDs in 1861. In many fields a PhD is required for employment as a university professor, researcher or scientist. Holders use the title Doctor, and the degree is often abbreviated PhD, or Ph.D. in North America.

Nonfiction [[Film|motion picture]] intended to document reality for instruction, education or maintaining a historical record. Documentary photography preceded the genre, as in the conflict photography of Mathew Brady during the [[American Civil War]]. Early documentaries, called actuality films, often lasted a minute or less and had no narrative structure. Over time they grew longer and covered more categories of information, from explicitly educational works to observational films and docufiction, which includes clearly fictional drama. The word "documentary" was coined by John Grierson in 1926, who defined the genre as the "creative treatment of actuality." Critics argue that selective editing and omitted context can distort the record. [[Social media|Social media]] platforms such as [[YouTube]] and Dailymotion have expanded documentary distribution and helped the genre reach audiences past certain forms of [[Censorship|censorship]].

Polyhedron with twelve flat faces. The regular dodecahedron is a [[Platonic solid]] with 12 regular pentagonal faces, 30 edges and 20 vertices, and three faces meet at each vertex. [[Plato]] associated it with the cosmos. Its geometry is intimately connected to the [[Golden ratio|golden ratio]], and its dual is the regular icosahedron. Some non-regular dodecahedra occur as crystal forms, such as the pyritohedron, a common crystal form of [[Pyrite|pyrite]].

Extinct flightless bird endemic to [[Mauritius]]. A member of the pigeon and dove family, the dodo was about 62.6–75 cm tall and may have weighed 10.6–17.5 kg in the wild. Its closest relative was the also-extinct Rodrigues solitaire, and its closest living relative is the Nicobar pigeon. Dutch sailors first recorded it in 1598. Hunting by sailors and [[Invasive species|invasive species]], along with habitat destruction, drove it to [[Extinction|extinction]], and the last widely accepted sighting was in 1662. Its appearance is known only from drawings, paintings and 17th-century accounts. Its disappearance less than a century after discovery drew attention to human involvement in the loss of species, and it became a symbol of extinction in popular culture after its role in *Alice's Adventures in Wonderland*.

Former landmass beneath the southern [[North Sea]]. Repeatedly exposed by lower sea levels during glacial periods, it connected [[Great Britain]] with continental Europe in the late [[Pleistocene|Pleistocene]] and early [[Holocene]] after the last glaciation. Rising seas inundated it between 10,000 and 7,000 years ago, leaving the Dogger Bank as a remnant. Most archaeological evidence of human habitation dates to the [[Mesolithic]] period. Fishing vessels have dredged up remains of mammoths and lions, along with prehistoric tools and weapons.

Rear-entry [[Sex position|sex position]] in which the receiving partner bends over or crouches on all fours, or lies on the abdomen. The term presumably refers to the posture of dogs mating, and in [[Ancient Rome|ancient Rome]] the practice was called *coitus more ferarum*, Latin for "sexual intercourse in the manner of wild beasts." The posture resembles lordosis behavior in female mammals. Compared with the [[Missionary position|missionary position]], it may allow the penis to penetrate deeper, with greater contact with the posterior wall of the vagina.

Capital and largest city of [[Qatar]], on the [[Persian Gulf|Persian Gulf]] coast. It is the country's main financial hub, and over 80% of Qatar's population lives in Doha or its surrounding suburbs. Founded in the 1820s as an offshoot of Al Bidda, it was declared the national capital in 1971, when Qatar gained independence from being a British protectorate. The city hosted the first ministerial-level meeting of the Doha Development Round of [[World Trade Organization]] negotiations, the 2006 [[Asian Games]] and the 2022 FIFA World Cup, and it will host the 2027 FIBA Basketball World Cup. Its name is said to derive from the Arabic *dohat*, meaning "roundness," a reference to the rounded bays of the coastline.

Model, typically of a human or humanoid figure, often used as a child's toy. Dolls have also been used in traditional religious rituals. The earliest examples were made of clay, stone, wood, bone, ivory or leather, and wooden paddle dolls have been found in Egyptian tombs dating to as early as the 21st century BC. Greek girls dedicated their dolls to [[Artemis]] at marriage, and Roman rag dolls have been found dating back to 300 BC. Modern doll manufacturing developed in [[Germany]] from the 15th century, and industrialization brought mass production in porcelain and plastic. *Akuaba* are wooden ritual fertility dolls from [[Ghana]]. Daruma dolls represent [[Bodhidharma]] and are used as good luck charms. The [[Barbie|Barbie]] doll, introduced in 1959, has become a global mass-market toy.

American singer-songwriter, actress and philanthropist, known as the "Queen of Country." She was one of the most successful performers in the history of [[Country music|country music]], with more than 100 million records sold. She wrote more than 3,000 songs and released 49 studio albums, beginning with her 1967 debut, *Hello, I'm Dolly*. Her songs include "I Will Always Love You," "Jolene," "Coat of Many Colors" and "9 to 5." Parton starred in the films *9 to 5* (1980) and *Steel Magnolias* (1989), and she has received eleven [[Grammy Awards|Grammy Awards]]. Her program Dolly Parton's Imagination Library, launched in 1995, has given more than 300 million free books to children from birth to age five, promoting [[Literacy|literacy]].

Female Finn-Dorset sheep, the first mammal cloned from an adult somatic cell. Her creators at the Roslin Institute in Scotland used nuclear transfer from a mammary gland cell, showing that a mature cell could produce a whole animal. The work advanced [[Stem cell|stem cell]] research, including the discovery of induced pluripotent stem cells. She lived at the Roslin Institute, produced several lambs and was euthanized at age six because of a progressive lung disease. Her body is exhibited at the National Museum of Scotland. The name was a reference to [[Dolly Parton]].

Mountain range in northeastern [[Italy]], part of the Southern Limestone Alps. Named after the carbonate rock dolomite, the range was declared a [[UNESCO]] World Heritage Site in 2009. Its highest peak is Marmolada, at 3,343 meters. During [[World War I]], the front line between Italian and Austro-Hungarian forces ran through the range. Many visitors climb the *vie ferrate*, protected paths through rock walls created during the war. The range is a center for [[Mountaineering]] and [[Skiing|skiing]].
